config.system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

position.recommendation: Stay with professional kitchens as the main business. Do not build a full home-cook product now. If the board wants to learn about home demand, run the proposed deposit test (EUR 14,000 of the EUR 20,000 budget, six weeks) and make any consumer move conditional on its result.

frame.objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep focusing on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify either choice.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or insider intentions
Search budget of 8 searches (7 left after read_brief); must read at least three sources
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Partly public financial data: note what cannot be found or reconciled
Must first establish how far RATIONAL already reaches individual buyers, not assume it
alternatives: No expansion: remain focused on professional commercial kitchens (status quo)
Consumer product: develop a home-cook version of combi-steamer technology sold direct to households
Route-to-market change: keep the same product but sell to home cooks via existing retail or online channels
Adjacent customer group: small professional or prosumer segments (caterers, bakeries, premium restaurants, serious home enthusiasts) rather than mass home cooks
Partnership or licensing: license the core steam/combi technology to an appliance maker for a home product, keeping the professional business
Hybrid: a small consumer line used to build brand and data while the core stays commercial

T1.claim: Home cooks who want restaurant-quality results but lack skill would pay a premium for a combi-steamer sold as an easy-to-use appliance, so RATIONAL could earn premium margins by controlling the design and brand of a home version of its existing steam-and-convection technology.
T1.who_benefits: Affluent home cooks and serious amateurs who want consistent results; RATIONAL, if it captures the premium margin and brand halo.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Steam-convection cooking removes much of the skill and timing guesswork that home cooks face, so the professional technology becomes a visible reason to buy rather than a technical spec.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL sells a branded home unit direct or through premium retail at a price above mass kitchen appliances, keeping design, software and service in-house.
assumptions: Home cooks will pay a large premium over mass appliances for professional-grade results
Kitchen space and installation do not block purchase at the target price
RATIONAL can build consumer distribution and support without damaging its professional brand
The commercial technology can be shrunk and made cheaply enough for a home price point
predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a home unit at the target price is high among affluent cooks who already own premium appliances
Pre-orders or deposits at a test price exceed a set threshold in a landing-page test
Buyers cite ease of consistent results rather than professional credentials as the main reason to buy
T1.first_claim: Home cooks who want restaurant-quality results but lack skill would pay a premium for a combi-steamer sold as an easy-to-use appliance, so RATIONAL could earn premium margins by controlling the design and brand of a home version of its existing steam-and-convection technology.

T2.claim: Home cooking is used too infrequently and in too constrained a space for a commercial-grade combi-steamer to earn back its cost, so a consumer product would sell in small volumes and mainly serve as a brand showcase; the professional business keeps the real value.
T2.who_benefits: Professional kitchens, which keep RATIONAL's focus, service network and margins; home buyers gain little beyond novelty.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Home cooks cook a few times a week, value counter space and simplicity, and compare a combi-steamer against cheaper multi-cookers, so the purchase rarely reaches the price where a premium unit pays back.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL stays with commercial sales, where a unit is used all day and the return on investment is measurable; any home activity earns little beyond brand awareness.
assumptions: Home use frequency is far below commercial use, so per-use value is low
Home buyers are price-sensitive relative to the cost of a professional-grade unit
Space and installation constraints limit the addressable home market
Competing home appliances already cover most of the steam-cooking use case
predictions: Stated purchase intent falls sharply once the price is shown alongside alternatives
Home buyers who own a multi-cooker rarely cite a need the combi-steamer would meet
Consumer-line sales stay a small share of total revenue even after launch
T2.first_claim: Home cooking is used too infrequently and in too constrained a space for a commercial-grade combi-steamer to earn back its cost, so a consumer product would sell in small volumes and mainly serve as a brand showcase; the professional business keeps the real value.

assessments.quote: On February 6, 2017, Anova was acquired by Electrolux , a home appliance company, for a total of US$250 million.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a different company selling a cheaper sous-vide device, not RATIONAL. It shows that a home appliance maker paid for a precision-cooking brand, which makes a premium home niche look commercially valuable. It does not show that home cooks would buy a combi-steamer, what they would pay, or whether RATIONAL could sell one.

assessments.quote: Combi ovens (iCombi product line) generate approximately 90% of Rational's appliance sales, while about 10% comes from the iVario series and newly added iHexagon appliances.
assessments.does_not_show: The source gives a product-mix share, not customer type, so it does not show that sales are professional or that home use is weak. It is a secondary summary with an unknown date. It cannot test whether a home unit would pay back. It only shows that the company's appliance revenue is concentrated in one product family.

assessments.quote: These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.
assessments.does_not_show: The source does not give sales volumes, brands, prices, geography or whether home buyers use these units often. It says nothing about RATIONAL, and a cheaper countertop unit may not show that a premium professional-grade home unit would pay back. It weakens my claim that home use is too rare or space-limited to justify a product, but does not settle it.

X1.name: Premium home unit landing-page and deposit test
X1.method: Run a paid-traffic landing page for a home combi-steamer concept shown at three proposed price points, with a refundable deposit option. Use a fictitious brand or unlabelled concept so intent is not biased by the RATIONAL name. Also include a short survey on current appliances and cooking frequency.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 qualified visitors from German-speaking and Dutch home-cooking audiences who own premium kitchen appliances (estimated, to be checked against actual traffic costs).
X1.measure: Share of visitors who place a refundable deposit at each price point; stated purchase intent; reported cooking frequency per week; reason for not buying.

prediction_by_theory.T1: A meaningful share of qualified visitors deposit at the premium price, with deposits stable across the top price point and the main stated reason being consistent results rather than credentials.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Deposits fall sharply as price rises, most visitors cook only a few times a week, and the main stated reasons are counter space, cost against multi-cookers and no clear need.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 2% of qualified visitors deposit at the premium price and at least half of depositors say they cook 4 or more times a week, keep T1 and scope a consumer prototype. If below 0.5% at premium price, or most cook under twice a week, reject T1 and stay with professional kitchens. Between these, keep both open and run a second test.

revisions.reason: No real evidence was added this round. The only new item is a SIMULATED what-if on installation coordination, which I have not used as evidence. T1 stays open and untested. The countertop combi-steamer source weakens T2's space argument but says nothing about RATIONAL or premium pricing.

I considered SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE as a what-if only. It is a SIMULATED result and I do not cite it as evidence. Even if it were real, it concerns installation friction in one recruited group, not the home use frequency or cost-to-value that T2 depends on, so it would not change T2. T2 stays the favoured theory on the thin real evidence, and the deposit test is still the decisive next step.

What-if only, per the stage instruction: if SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE were real, it would show that installation coordination changes reservations in one recruited group (72 vs 32 per 400). For T1 that means only that premium-buyer friction matters, and the test is about a bundled service, not about the appliance's demand or price. It would not confirm that home cooks pay a premium for the product. Nothing here is real data; I do not change my belief and I do not cite it in the finish.

final.recommendation: Stay focused on professional kitchens. Do not build a full home-cook product now. Before any consumer move, run the proposed refundable-deposit test (about EUR 14,000 of the EUR 20,000 budget, six weeks) and let its pre-agreed threshold decide.
final.target_customer: Professional kitchens remain the target. Home cooks are an unproven, separate test, not a current segment.
final.value_proposition: For professional kitchens: the combi-steamer's measurable performance in daily commercial use. No home value proposition is supported by the evidence I read.
final.next_action: Scope the proposed landing-page and deposit test with an unlabelled concept at three price points, and agree thresholds before running it: keep the consumer option open only if at least 2% of qualified visitors deposit at the premium price and at least half of depositors cook four or more times a week (both proposed, not observed).
final.uncertainty: Home-demand evidence is very thin. No source I read measures home buyers, willingness to pay or home use frequency. The 4.8 million figure is a company estimate. The 90% iCombi share is a secondary summary of unknown date. Anova's sale is an analogy. I could not find or reconcile RATIONAL's financial data by channel or customer type. No SIMULATED result is used as evidence.
would_change_if: The deposit test clears the proposed thresholds at the premium price, with depositors reporting frequent use
Public data shows premium countertop combi-steamers selling in volume near a professional unit's cost
RATIONAL's own disclosures show a home or prosumer channel reaching individual buyers at scale
Reliable data shows professional demand saturating, leaving growth only in adjacent segments
A licensing partner offers a home product that needs no RATIONAL capital or brand risk

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The only new item is a SIMULATED what-if (installation-coordination offer test). It is not real data, so I do not use it as evidence and do not change my belief. Even if it were real, it would bear on installation friction within one recruited group, not on whether home cooks would pay a premium for a combi-steamer at scale. T1 stays open and untested, as before.

arguments.uncertainty: Home-demand evidence is very thin. No source I read measures home buyers, willingness to pay or home use frequency. The 4.8 million figure is a company estimate. The 90% iCombi share is a secondary summary of unknown date. Anova's sale is an analogy. I could not find or reconcile RATIONAL's financial data by channel or customer type. No SIMULATED result is used as evidence.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.
